etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English catirpel, catirpeller, probably from Old Northern French catepeluse (Modern French chatte + pileuse (“hairy cat”)), from Late Latin catta + pilōsa. The sense "rapacious, extortionate person" arose by association with obsolete piller (“plunderer”).

definitions.definition: The larva of a butterfly or moth; leafworm.
A vehicle with a caterpillar track; a crawler.
(mathematics) A set of subtrees of a tree.
(obsolete) A rapacious, extortionate person preying upon the community.

quote.citation: 1595 December 9 (first known performance), William Shakespeare, “The life and death of King Richard the Second”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies: Published According to the True Originall Copies (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene iii], page 33:
quote.text: Bristow Castle, which they say is heldBy Busbie, Bagot, and their Complices,The Caterpillers of the Commonwealth,Which I haue sworne to weed, and plucke away.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To move along slowly, drawing one's body up, in the manner of a caterpillar.
